Give captured Gaussians stable world identity

A splat renderer answers an image question: which color and opacity does this primitive contribute at a pixel? Editing a captured scene asks a different question: which persistent world element does this primitive represent, and which physical variables are allowed to move it? These representations overlap, but they are not interchangeable. The original 3D Gaussian Splatting work optimizes anisotropic primitives for view synthesis and rendering; the entity and motion contract below is an explicit engine extension, not a property guaranteed by a trained PLY file. The 3D Gaussian Splatting paper

Keep identity separate from storage order. Let each Gaussian carry an immutable identifier , where is a namespace or asset identifier and is a local identifier. The current vector index is only a temporary address. Sorting, compaction, filtering, or cloning may change that address; none of those operations may silently change the identity of an existing record. A lookup table maps to the current index and is rebuilt after a reorder. A newly cloned primitive receives a new identifier and records its parent ID; it does not reuse the parent’s ID.

An editable scene needs a second relation from Gaussian IDs to semantic entities and physical degrees of freedom. Represent it as a versioned association table. For Gaussian and entity or node , let be the authored influence weight. For a Gaussian fully assigned to one rigid object, one weight is . For a soft boundary, several weights may be nonzero. Within one declared support set, require

Normalization is necessary to reproduce a common translation. Reproducing a complete affine map also requires the rest-center reconstruction below, or an explicitly retained local offset. It does not prove that the association is correct: confidence, source, and an unassigned state must remain explicit. Do not turn a low-confidence semantic guess into a collider or a destructive edit automatically.

Couple edits in both directions and keep their proof

An appearance edit and a physical edit are separate operations with an explicit bridge between them. In one direction, a semantic selection resolves stable entity IDs to stable Gaussian IDs, then maps those Gaussian IDs through the versioned support table to affected physical DOFs. In the other direction, a committed physical state computes the local motion map for each supported Gaussian, updates its mean and covariance, and rebuilds projected bounds and tile references before rendering. A translation need not change an object-attached appearance function in this model. For spherical-harmonic (SH) appearance attached to a frame , evaluate its coefficients using local viewing direction , and rotate with the object. A renderer that instead stores world-direction coefficients must explicitly choose whether to preserve that world-space function or rotate its basis to follow the object. Deformation and relighting do not have an automatic appearance solution. Keep the appearance frame separate from the covariance eigenbasis: repeated eigenvalues and eigenvector sign choices can change that basis without changing the Gaussian shape.

To store a general deformed covariance back as rotation and scales, diagonalize the symmetric , require positive eigenvalues, and use scales . Choose eigenvector signs so before converting to a quaternion. At repeated eigenvalues, orientation is not unique; preserve continuity or retain the full covariance rather than interpreting an arbitrary eigenvector flip as physical rotation. Covariance push-forward changes shape, not a conserved physical mass. If opacity is an appearance peak it may be held fixed by policy; preserving an extinction or density integral needs a separately defined field and Jacobian rule. Do not silently assume either policy from .

A useful edit transaction has a before state, a proposed state, and a commit decision. Store the edit ID, parent scene revision, selected stable IDs, association-table revision, operator and parameters, before/after state hashes, affected Gaussian IDs, and validation results. Write the candidate state to a separate revision. Validate finite means, normalized orientation, positive-definite covariance, valid support weights, and stable ID uniqueness before publication. Render the candidate from the same cameras used for the before state. Compare the intended region and the declared unaffected region separately; include color, depth and dominant-ID checks where available. Commit the new revision only if all declared conditions pass. Otherwise retain the prior revision and the failed report. A provenance record makes a result repeatable; it does not make the physical interpretation true by itself.

Before commit, check IDs are unique, every affected support row remains nonnegative and sums to one, means are finite, each covariance is finite and positive definite, and the candidate render preserves declared unaffected regions within the chosen color/depth/ID tolerances. A Gaussian is a learned appearance primitive, not automatically a surface point, rigid body, collider, or mass element. An association table is a model chosen for an application, and ambiguous or incomplete support should remain visible as uncertainty. The affine covariance rule preserves a Gaussian footprint under a locally affine map; it does not solve visibility, self-intersection, cloth topology, contact, or appearance changes caused by newly revealed surfaces. A render that matches the original cameras cannot prove an edit is physically correct from unseen views.

Before calling a captured-world edit complete, a learner should be able to: trace a semantic selection through stable IDs after reordering; show that normalized support weights reproduce a shared affine transform; derive and calculate ; identify a rank-deficient local fit; rotate or preserve SH according to a stated frame; and produce a provenance record plus before/after tests for affected and unaffected regions. The original 3DGS paper establishes a view-synthesis representation and renderer, not these editor, physics, or publication contracts. Those are additional systems that must be designed and verified explicitly.
Train the splats only after the forward renderer is understood

A projected, tiled, ordered, composited image is now a complete forward result, and the preceding CPU/GPU comparison gives us checks for color, depth, dominant ID, tile occupancy, and sorting. We can now ask the inverse question: how should the stored splats change so that this renderer matches calibrated photographs? This is where training belongs in the story: the forward map and its failure signals are already visible. The original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper starts from sparse points from camera calibration when available, optimizes their attributes, and interleaves optimization with density control. A rasterizer tutorial without this lifecycle explains only inference, not how the captured representation is fitted. (Kerbl et al., 2023 paper)

The author implementation used below is pinned to commit 54c035f7834b564019656c3e3fcc3646292f727d, committed 30 October 2024. It is a precise historical source specimen, not a claim about every later fork or current 3DGS implementation. Its train.py uses a weighted and structural-similarity image loss, optionally adds depth regularization, differentiates the loss, gathers projected-mean gradient statistics, performs scheduled density control and opacity reset, then steps the optimizer. Its GaussianModel maps stored scale through , opacity through , and normalizes rotation quaternions. A robust importer or optimizer must still reject or explicitly repair a zero quaternion: normalization alone does not turn a zero vector into a valid rotation.

In the pinned training loop, the image term is a weighted plus DSSIM loss; when reliable depth supervision is enabled, a weighted inverse-depth term is added. The objective’s exact weights and preprocessing are part of the experiment. Lower image error does not prove unique or physically useful geometry: several scenes can explain the same measurements, and a view-synthesis representation can exploit appearance to hide geometric error.

Density control changes model size between gradient steps

Continuous optimization cannot add a primitive when current support is inadequate. The pinned implementation accumulates the norm of the first two components of the projected-mean gradient for visible Gaussians and divides by a visibility count to estimate an average image-space signal (add_densification_stats). At scheduled intervals it applies two capacity operations:

ListItem.Content: • Clone: when the accumulated mean-gradient magnitude reaches the threshold and the largest world-space scale is no greater than percent_dense * scene_extent, copy that small primitive’s mean, appearance, opacity, scale, and rotation into a new primitive. The original remains. This adds local representation capacity without moving either copy.

• Split: when the gradient reaches threshold but the largest scale exceeds that cutoff, replace the broad primitive with children. In this pinned code by default. It samples a zero-mean offset whose standard deviation is the parent’s three scales, rotates that offset by the parent’s rotation, and adds it to the mean. Child scales are divided by before mapping back through the inverse scale activation. Then the parent is removed. The samples are random in the parent’s anisotropic local coordinates; the reference does not deterministically split along the single largest axis.

Chapter.Content: The cited source performs clone first and split second. It then prunes primitives whose opacity is below the scheduled minimum; after the configured size gate it also prunes those whose recorded screen radius is too large or whose maximum world scale exceeds times the scene extent. It finally resets scheduled opacities by capping decoded opacity at , mapping back to logits, and resetting that parameter group’s Adam moments. Those are choices of this revision, not universal constants or a claim that every fork follows them. (densify_and_prune, split and clone; reset_opacity)

The training-loop ordering matters. At the cited revision, loss.backward() runs first. Inside the no-gradient control block, the program accumulates visible gradient/radius statistics, performs any scheduled clone/split/prune, performs any scheduled opacity reset (also at the first density-control iteration for a white background), and only then calls the exposure and Gaussian optimizer steps and clears gradients. It does not do optimizer-step-then-density-edit as a generic pseudocode might suggest (train.py, lines 142 and 163–186).

The model code must keep variable-length tensors and optimizer state aligned. When it appends children, it appends zero rows to Adam’s exp_avg and exp_avg_sq; when pruning, it slices those moments by the same keep-mask; opacity reset replaces the opacity parameter and zeros that parameter’s two moment tensors (GaussianModel, lines 316–405). This revision constructs new Parameter objects during append/prune/reset and does not transfer the just-backpropagated .grad tensor to those replacements. Consequently, on an edit step those replaced groups have no gradient for the immediately following optimizer call; their stored Adam moments are preserved/sliced or reset as the code specifies, and the next render/backward populates gradients for the new parameters. This behavior follows from the pinned PyTorch code path; it is an implementation fact to verify again when changing frameworks or revisions.

A small branch trace (numbers are teaching values, not source defaults): average projected-mean gradients are , largest world scales are , and the example gradient threshold is with a small/large cutoff of . The first splat stays; the second splits; the third clones. If the second has opacity and the example opacity floor is , its children may be created by the clone/split operation and then removed by the later prune mask if they inherit that low opacity. A faithful trace must apply the implementation’s actual sequence, rather than silently moving the opacity prune ahead of growth. For each append, initialize child moments to zero; for parent removal, slice all parameter and per-splat statistic arrays with the same keep-mask. This example teaches the branch and ordering, not expected quality or useful production thresholds.

Represent the optimizer state and the topology schedule in a checkpoint, not just the visible means and colors. A reproducible experiment records calibrated cameras, image preparation, loss weights, optimizer type and learning-rate schedule, random seed, density thresholds and intervals, opacity-reset schedule, source revision, held-out views, memory use, and render/training time. The pinned loop tests held-out cameras when configured, but the selection and metric must be recorded; a test view used repeatedly to tune the model is no longer an untouched final evaluation.

The following complete Python program checks the two-splat color/logit derivatives against 240 finite differences, rejects the tempting wrong footprint chain rule, verifies a small SGD step, and tests stable identity and optimizer-moment alignment during a declared prune/clone policy. Run it with python3 tools/labs/gaussian_training_step_lab.py or with python3 -O tools/labs/gaussian_training_step_lab.py. It models one scalar pixel with fixed footprint and ordering; it does not train geometry, reproduce Graphdeco topology ordering, or validate GPU gradients.
